Thesis outline
This thesis proposes a new approach to deriving cooperative solution concepts
from dynamic interactive learning models. For diﬀerent classes of coopera-
tive games, the procedures implement the core. Within the core, tendencies
towards equity are revealed and equitable outcomes are favoured in the long
run.
Chapter 1. Motivation
Most of cooperative game theory is static, including solution concepts such
as the core, Shapley value and the Nash bargaining solution.
To support
these solutions, dynamic implementation procedures have been proposed. In
these models, multistage bargaining games or dynamic noncooperative games
are played and the cooperative solution is implemented via equilibria of these
related games. In contrast to existing approaches, we propose a class of fully
dynamic models of learning based solely on each individual’s assessment of
how well he did in the past. These procedures reveal internal bias towards
stable and equitable outcomes.
Chapter 2. Evolutionary cooperative bargaining
Many agents repeatedly bargain over a cooperative surplus. Agents feel their
way to Pareto-eﬃcient outcomes in a nonstrategic manner by incremental ad-
justments to their demand and aspiration levels. Transfers of surplus shares in
between any two agents are always possible but the procedures reveal global
tendencies away from substantial levels of inequity over time. This leads to
the long-run implementation of equal splits of the surplus most of the time.
In the intermediate run, however, the adjustment processes are considerably
more complex. With growth in the possibility frontier, expected inequity may
initially rise and only fall as the possibility frontier reaches a stable long-run
position.
Chapter 3. Assignment games with trial-and-error
Many separate pairs of agents from two sides of a market may form. Partner-
ships are broken time and again, reshuﬄed and restored. Players experiment
with various partnerships before settling on optimal partners. The dynamics
reveal that, over time, matching becomes more and more stable. Most of the
time, optimal partnerships form and share the gains in a pairwise stable way.
Loss-averse partners share close to ﬁfty-ﬁfty with high probability, unless one
or both of the partners have more proﬁtable outside alternatives.

The classic paper of Shapley and Shubik \cite{Shapley1971assignment} characterized the core of the assignment game. We observe that a sub-coalition consisting of one player (or a set of players from the same side of the bipartition) can make zero profit, and therefore its profit under a core imputation can be an arbitrary amount. Hence an arbitrary core imputation makes {\em no fairness guarantee at the level of individual agents}. Can this deficiency be addressed by picking a ``good'' core imputation? To arrive at an appropriate solution concept, we give specific criteria for picking a special core imputation, and we undertake a detailed comparison of four solution concepts. Leximin and leximax core imputations come out as clear winners; we define these to be {\em equitable core imputations}. These imputations achieve ``fairness'' in different ways: whereas leximin tries to make poor agents more rich, leximax tries to make rich agents less rich. We give combinatorial strongly polynomial algorithms for computing these imputations via a novel adaptation of the classical primal-dual paradigm. The ``engine'' driving them involves insights into core imputations obtained via complementarity. It will not be surprising if our work leads to new uses of this powerful technique. Furthermore, we expect more work on computing the leximin and leximax core imputations of other natural games, in addition to the recent follow-up work \cite{Leximin-max}.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Most of the existing results for one-to-one assignment markets cannot be extended to the many-to-many assignment markets [20, 21]: some core allocations may not be supported by competitive prices and the core may not be a lattice. However, for the many-to-one assignment games, the core retains desirable properties such as non-emptiness and a lattice structure based on the partial order on the set of payoffs to the side of the market where agents have unitary capacity. This guarantees in that case the existence of an optimal core allocation for each side of the market. Yet, not all classical solution concepts behave as well in this setting. Atay et al. [2] recently show that even for many-to-one assignment markets the bargaining set does not necessarily coincide with the core and that the kernel may not be contained within the core. While classical results have focused on the existence and side-optimality of core allocations, less attention has been paid to the full set of the vertices of the core polytope. In this paper, we study the structure of the core polytope in many-to-one assignment games.

L44: # Fair Core Imputations for the Assignment Game:
L45: New Solution Concepts and Efficient Algorithms
L46: 
L47: Vijay V. Vazirani Note: Supported in part by NSF grant CCF-2230414. Affiliation: University of California, Irvine
L48: ###### Abstract
L49: 
L50: The assignment game is a classical model for profit-sharing and a cornerstone of cooperative game theory. While an imputation in its core guarantees fairness among coalitions, it provides no fairness guarantee at the level of individual agents: single agents or one-sided coalitions have zero standalone value and may receive arbitrarily small payoffs. Motivated by the growing focus on individual-level fairness, we ask: Can one select a core imputation that is also fair to individuals?
L51: We introduce three individual-fairness-driven solution concepts, each promoting equity in a different way. The leximin and leximax core imputations extend max–min and min–max fairness to uplift the least advantaged and constrain the most advantaged agents, respectively. The min-spread core imputation minimizes the gap between the largest and smallest positive payoffs, promoting equitable profit distribution.
L52: For all three solution concepts, we develop combinatorial, strongly polynomial algorithms. The leximin and leximax algorithms are based on a novel adaptation of the primal–dual paradigm, while the min-spread algorithm combines partial executions of the first two. We expect our work to revive innovation on the potent primal-dual paradigm as well as promote further work on the algorithmic study of fairness and stability.
L53: ## 1 Introduction
L54: Fairness and equitable division have long been central themes in economics, from early social choice theory [cite32†2 ] to modern challenges in Internet resource allocation [cite33†37 ]. The study of fairness has come to a basic truth: no single definition can universally capture fairness, e.g., [cite34†40 ] lists 21 definitions! Within this vast literature, we are concerned with fairness at the level of coalitions and individual fairness.
L55: For the former, the core is the gold standard solution concept: it ensures that no coalition has an incentive to secede by guaranteeing each coalition at least as much profit as they can achieve on their own. Hence a core imputation guarantees stability by allocating a fair profit to each of exponentially many coalitions—a stringent requirement indeed.
L56: Recent work across game theory, networking and resource allocation has renewed attention on individual-level fairness as a fundamental consideration, e.g., the wide spread use of max-min and min-max fairness [cite35†41 , cite36†7 , cite37†39 , cite38†43 ], as well as their extensions to leximin and leximax allocations in modern applications such as fair rent division [cite39†18 ] and citizens’ assemblies [cite40†15 ].
L57: Our work bridges these two traditions in the context of the assignment game, which occupies a central place within cooperative game theory; the classic work of Shapley and Shubik [cite41†47 ] gave a complete characterization of its core, see Section cite10†3.1 . In this game, a coalition consisting of a single agent or a group from one side of the bipartition has zero standalone value.
L58: Consequently, under an arbitrary core imputation, individual agents are allowed to receive arbitrary profit shares, leading to inequity. To address this deficiency, we seek a core imputation that satisfies two key criteria:
L59:   1. 1.
L60: 
L61: The allocation of profit shares is individually fair.
L62: 
L63:   2. 2.
L64: 
L65: It is computable in polynomial—or preferably, strongly polynomial—time via a combinatorial algorithm^{1}^{1} 1 That is, the algorithm does not invoke an LP-solver, e.g., see [cite42†46 , cite43†33 ].
L66: We propose three solution concepts. All three deal with profit shares of essential agents, i.e., agents which are matched in every maximum weight matching, see Section cite11†4 ; these are the only agents which get positive profits in core imputations.
L67: 
L68:   1. 1.
L69: 
L70: the leximin core imputation, which extends max-min fairness by maximizing the smallest individual share and, subject to that, the next smallest, and so on;
L71: 
L72:   2. 2.
L73: the leximax core imputation, which symmetrically extends min-max fairness by minimizing the largest share, then the second largest, and so on;
L74: 
L75:   3. 3.
L76: 
L77: the min-spread core imputation, which minimizes the difference between the largest and smallest profit shares of essential agents.
L78: It is easy to see that none of these solution concepts dominates the others, e.g., see the example given in Section cite15†5 . Our solution concepts seek to reconcile the tension between coalitions demanding profit which is commensurate with their inherent worth and the societal norm of “equality” as a desirable outcome.
L79: Each promotes individual fairness in a distinct way: leximin uplifts the least advantaged, leximax reins in the most advantaged and min-spread makes individual profit shares as equal as possible. In Section cite15†5 we show that whereas leximin and leximax core imputations are unique, min-spread is not. In Section cite16†5.1 we show that the prominent solution concept of nucleolus does not promote individual fairness in any of these three ways, even for an infinite family of games, Theorem cite44†6 .
L80: We design combinatorial, strongly polynomial algorithms, having a running time of $O(mn^{3})$, for all three proposed solution concepts. For the leximin and leximax core imputations, our algorithms are based on a novel adaptation of the classical primal-dual paradigm; see Section cite7†1.1 . The algorithm for the min-spread solution is arguably even more innovative.
L81: It is made possible by the combinatorial nature of the previous two algorithms and is obtained by carefully orchestrating their partial executions, see Section cite27†10 .
L82: The assignment and stable matching games share a key structural property: in both, the set of solutions forms a distributive lattice, with the top and bottom elements favoring opposite sides of the bipartition (see details in Section cite8†2 ). These extreme solutions are efficiently computable in both settings. However, while the stable matching lattice is finite—enabling the design of algorithms for finding more equitable outcomes—the lattice of core imputations in the assignment game is infinite.
L83: This fundamental difference precludes the use of Birkhoff’s Representation Theorem and necessitates a fundamentally new approach to identifying individually fair core imputations.
L84: We anticipate that the novel way of running the primal-dual method proposed here will not only be exploited for additional applications, but it will also revive innovation on this highly potent method^{2}^{2} 2 This is the reason we preferred submitting this paper to a theory, rather than an AGT, conference.. Additionally, we expect our work to promote further work on the algorithmic study of fairness and stability, as was done in [cite45†20 ].
L85: ### 1.1 How was the Primal-Dual Framework Adapted to our Problem?
L86: 
L87: The primal-dual method has three distinguishing features:
L88: 
L89:   1. 1.
L90: 
L91: It provides a flexible, high level framework whose details can be tailored to the specific problem at hand.
L92: 
L93:   2. 2.
L94: 
L95: It achieves global optimality or near-optimality through a sequence of local improvements.
L96: 
L97:   3. 3.
L98: 
L99: It leads to efficient, combinatorial algorithms.
L100: The method achieved major successes, first in combinatorial optimization [cite43†33 , cite42†46 ] and then in approximation algorithms [cite46†51 ]. These settings involved finding an integral optimal (or near-optimal) solution to the primal LP, together with an optimal (or near-optimal) solution to the dual LP. Complementary slackness conditions — or an appropriate relaxation of these conditions — helped transform the global task into a sequence of local tasks.
L101: Following these successes, researchers adapted it to solve rational convex programs, i.e., non-linear convex programs that always admit rational solutions, defined in [cite47†52 ]. These include [cite48†10 , cite49†28 , cite47†52 , cite50†11 ]. Indeed, today it is appropriate to call this method the primal-dual paradigm.
L102: Despite its versatility, it was not initially clear that this method would be suitable for our setting. In our case, computing an optimal solution to the primal and dual LPs — namely, a maximum-weight matching and an associated core imputation — is straightforward. However, the core challenge lies in transforming this arbitrary core imputation into the leximin or leximax core imputation.
L103: One might consider locally improving the imputation while maintaining the optimality of both primal and dual solutions. However, because the primal-dual pair satisfies all complementary slackness conditions, how will the global problem be broken into local steps? To address this, we introduce a novel coordinating mechanism: a clock that governs the algorithm’s progress and synchronizes all updates.
L104: For each time $t$, we can define a vertex set $W_{t}\subseteq(U\cup V)$ such that in the induced subgraph $H_{t}$ of $G$, the profit shares form the unique leximin core imputation for $H_{t}$^{3}^{3} 3 The proof of this fact crucially depends on the correct resolution of some subtle algorithmic choices, see Sections cite21†7.2 and cite23†7.4 .. We prove that in polynomial time $W_{t}=(U\cup V)$, hence terminating in the required imputation.
L105: The proof of this fact crucially depends on the correct resolution of some subtle algorithmic choices, see Sections cite21†7.2 and cite23†7.4 .
L106: While prior primal-dual algorithms have employed the notion of time, our use of it is distinct in both purpose and prominence. For example, in [cite51†27 ], dual variables evolve over time, but this evolution is used merely to enforce relaxed complementary slackness conditions, which remain the primary engine for local-to-global transformation. Similarly, in [cite49†28 ], time progression aids in ensuring cross-monotonicity in cost-sharing methods, rather than in structuring the optimization process itself.
L107: In contrast, in our approach, time is the central coordinating device that transforms the global optimization problem into a sequence of structured local updates.
L108: The broad outline given above is far from sufficient for designing the entire algorithm. The latter requires a precise understanding of the way core imputations allocate the total profit to agents and teams; in particular, we need to answer the following questions:
L109: 
L110:   1. 1.
L111: 
L112: Do core imputations spread the profit more-or-less evenly or do they restrict profit to certain well-chosen agents? If the latter, what characterizes these “chosen” agents?
L113: 
L114:   2. 2.
L115: An edge $(i,j)$ in the underlying graph is called a team. By definition, under any core imputation, the sum of profits of $i$ and $j$ is at least the weight of this edge. For which teams is the sum strictly larger?
L116: 
L117:   3. 3.
L118: 
L119: How do core imputations behave in the presence of degeneracy? An assignment game is said to be non-degenerate if it admits a unique maximum weight matching.
L120: 
L121: Our answers, using complementary slackness conditions and strict complementarity, are provided in Section cite11†4 .
L122: ## 2 Related Works
L123: Comparison with the stable matching game: A useful perspective is provided by the stable matching game of Gale and Shapley [cite52†19 ], which is a non-transferable utility (NTU) game. The core of this game is the set of all stable matchings — each ensures that no coalition formed by one agent from each side of the bipartition has an incentive to secede. It is well known that this set forms a finite distributive lattice.
L124: Its top and bottom elements maximally favor one side and disfavor the other side of the bipartition, and the Deferred Acceptance Algorithm [cite52†19 ] computes precisely these two extremes.
L125: However, in many applications, one desires stable matchings that are more equitable to both sides. This has motivated considerable research on finding such matchings efficiently, leading to efficient algorithms as well as intractability results, see [cite53†25 , cite54†50 , cite55†6 , cite56†5 , cite57†13 ]. L126: Shapley and Shubik [cite41†47 ] showed that the set of its core imputations is the entire polytope of optimal solutions to the dual of the LP-relaxation of the maximum weight matching problem in the underlying bipartite graph. If this set is not a singleton, it is a dense set consisting of uncountably many elements. Furthermore, this set forms an infinite distributive lattice.
L127: The top and bottom elements of this lattice form two extreme imputations, each maximally favoring one side and disfavoring the other side of the bipartition. So far efficient algorithms were known for computing only these two (least fair) imputations as outlined below^{4}^{4} 4 Their convex combination is also a core imputation; however, it is not clear what fairness properties it possesses.. L145: To deal with games having an empty core, the following two notions have been given. The first is that of least core, defined by Mascher et al. [cite74†34 ]. If the core is empty, there will necessarily be sets $S\subseteq V$ such that $v(S)<p(S)$ for any imputation $v$. The least core maximizes the minimum of $p(S)-v(S)$ over all sets $S\subseteq V$, subject to $v(\emptyset)=0$ and $v(V)=p(V)$.
L146: A more well known notion is that of nucleolus [cite75†45 ] which is contained in the least core, see Definition cite76†13 . For any imputation, $p$, define $p(S)-c(S)$ to be the surplus of coalition $\emptyset\subset S\subset V$. The idea behind the nucleolus is to spread the surplus as evenly as possible across all coalitions by picking the leximin imputation over the surplus of coalitions. The nucleolus always exists for any cooperative game, even if its core is empty and is unique.
L147: Furthermore, if the core of the game is non-empty, then the nucleolus lies in the core. Solymosi and Raghavan [cite77†48 ] gave a strongly polynomial algorithm for computing the nucleolus of the assignment game, see also Section cite15†5 .

L158:

L163: ### 3.1 The Results of Shapley and Shubik for the Assignment Game
L164: 
L165: The assignment game consists of a bipartite graph $G=(U,V,E)$ and a weight function for the edges $w:E\rightarrow\mathcal{Q}_{+}$, where we assume that each edge has positive weight; otherwise the edge can be removed from $G$. The agents of the game are the vertices, $U\cup V$ and the total worth of the game is the weight of a maximum weight matching in $G$; the latter needs to be distributed among the vertices.
L166: For this game, a coalition $(U^{\prime}\cup V^{\prime})$ consists of a subset of the agents, also called vertices, with $U^{\prime}\subseteq U$ and $V^{\prime}\subseteq V$. The worth of a coalition $(U^{\prime}\cup V^{\prime})$ is defined to be the weight of a maximum weight matching in the graph $G$ restricted to vertices in $(U^{\prime}\cup V^{\prime})$ and is denoted by $c(U^{\prime}\cup V^{\prime})$. The characteristic function of the game is defined to be $c:2^{U\cup V}\rightarrow\mathcal{Q}_{+}$.
L167: An imputation consists of two functions $u:{U}\rightarrow\mathcal{Q}_{+}$ and $v:{V}\rightarrow\mathcal{Q}_{+}$ such that $\sum_{i\in U}{u_{i}}+\sum_{j\in V}{v_{j}}=c(U\cup V)$. Imputation $(u,v)$ is said to be in the core of the assignment game if for any coalition $(U^{\prime}\cup V^{\prime})$, the total profit allocated to agents in the coalition is at least as large as the worth that they can generate by themselves, i.e., $\sum_{i\in U^{\prime}}{u_{i}}+\sum_{j\in V^{\prime}}{v_{j}}\geq c(S)$.

L83: In both our work and [cite46†4 , cite47†6 ], the dynamics are designed such that the core states are the absorbing states of the process. In particular, our learning dynamics explore coalition proposals until a stable, core outcome is found.
L84: Our dynamics also address the “remainder problem” posed in [cite43†28 ], which asks what happens to the remaining members of a coalition when some agents depart. In our model, agents in the remainder set become singletons. This is a natural consequence of our aspiration-based framework: the aspirations of the remaining agents might sum to more than the value of any smaller coalition they could form, making such a coalition infeasible.
L85: By becoming singletons, they retain their aspirations and remain available for future, potentially more valuable partnerships.
L86: Other related research has explored different notions of stability and dynamics. For instance, a recent paper presents online dynamics for tracking the core within a guaranteed bound in games with boundedly time-varying valuations [cite48†30 ]. An alternative stability concept, based on coalition split-and-merge processes, was studied in [cite49†3 ], with distributed dynamics that converge to this notion of stability introduced in [cite50†32 ].
L87: Finally, within the specific domain of B-matching, much of the literature has traditionally focused on centralized or distributed algorithms for finding optimal weighted matchings [cite51†20 , cite52†35 ], with less emphasis on the resulting value allocations. However, recent work, beginning with new characterizations of the core in [cite53†37 ], has brought a renewed focus to the game-theoretic properties of B-matchings.
L88: This new line of inquiry includes further foundational work characterizing the core and establishing the hardness of finding optimal core allocations [cite54†12 ], investigations into related concepts such as equitable core imputations [cite55†11 ], and an analysis of the special case of 2-matching games [cite56†34 ].
L89: Building on this cutting-edge research, our paper addresses the subsequent challenge: we contribute by providing distributed learning dynamics that not only form an efficient matching but also converge to a stable allocation within the core.

L92: ## 2 Transferable Utility Coalitional Games
L93: 
L94: Transferable utility coalitional games are defined by a set of agents and a value assigned to each possible coalition. This value represents the collective payoff that agents in a coalition can achieve by working together and can subsequently be distributed among them. In this section, we formally define TU coalitional games, the core of such games, and other relevant definitions and propositions.
L95: We follow the definition of TU coalitional games in [cite36†29 ], but broaden the definition of the core to include games in which forming the grand coalition, the coalition containing all agents, may lead to a suboptimal overall benefit for the agents. We then present the dynamics introduced in [cite37†14 ], which pertain to TU coalitional games, along with their convergence analysis.
L96: ### Definition 1
L97: 
L98: A transferable utility coalitional game (TU coalitional game) is defined by a pair \((N,\varphi ),\) where N is a finite set of agents, and \(\varphi :2^N\rightarrow \mathbb {R}_+\) is a valuation function for each possible subset of agents.
L99: ### Definition 2
L100: 
L101: A partition \(\pi\) of a set N is a set of disjoint subsets of N, such that
L102: 
L103: $$\begin{aligned}S \cap S'=\emptyset \ \text { for all } S,S'\in \pi \text { and } {N=\textstyle \bigcup \limits _{S\in \pi }}S.\end{aligned}$$
L104: 
L105: We denote the set of all partitions of N by \(\Pi (N)\)
L106: ### Definition 3
L107: 
L108: A core solution of a TU coalitional game \((N,\varphi )\) is a pair \(({x},\pi )\) consisting of an allocation vector \({x}\in \mathbb {R}_+^{|N|}\), which represents the payoff for each agent, and a partition of N that satisfies the following two conditions:
L109: 
L110:   * Coalitional Rationality:
L111: 
L112: $$\begin{aligned} \sum _{i \in S} x_i \geqslant \varphi (S)\ \quad \text {for all } S\subseteq N \end{aligned}$$
L113: 
L114:   * Efficiency:
L115: $$\begin{aligned}\sum _{i\in S}x_i = \varphi (S)\ \quad \text {for all }S \in \pi \end{aligned}$$
L116: 
L117: We denote the set of core solutions of the game \((N,\varphi )\) by \(\Psi .\)
L118: ### Example 1
L119: 
L120: (TU coalitional game and core solution) Let the set of agents be \(N = \{1, 2, 3\}\) and suppose the valuation function is defined as:
L121: 
L122: $$\begin{aligned} & \varphi (\{1\}) = 1,\quad \varphi (\{2\}) = 1,\quad \varphi (\{3\}) = 2, \\ & \varphi (\{1,2\}) = 3,\quad \varphi (\{1,3\}) = 3,\quad \varphi (\{2,3\}) = 3, \quad \varphi (N) = 2. \end{aligned}$$
L123: 
L124: Consider the allocation \({x} = (2, 1, 2)\) and the coalition structure \(\pi = \{\{1,2\}, \{3\}\}\). Then \(({x},\pi )\) satisfy
L125:   * Coalitional Rationality:
L126: 
L127:     * \(x_i \geqslant \varphi (\{i\})\) for all \(i\in N,\)
L128: 
L129:     * \(x_1+x_2=3 \geqslant \varphi (\{1,2\}),\ x_2+x_3=3 \geqslant \varphi (\{2,3\}),\ x_3+x_1=4 \geqslant \varphi (\{1,3\}),\)
L130: 
L131:     * \(x_1+x_2+x_3=5\geqslant \varphi (N)\).
L132: 
L133:   * Efficiency:
L134: 
L135:     * For \(\{1,2\}\), \(x_1 + x_2 = 3 = \varphi (\{1,2\})\),
L136: 
L137:     * For \(\{3\}\), \(x_3 = 2 = \varphi (\{3\})\).
L138: 
L139: Hence, \(({x}, \pi ) \in \Psi\) is a core solution.

L1312: Ultimately, our findings demonstrate the potential for autonomous agents in distributed systems to achieve stable, efficient outcomes, even with limited information and under dynamic conditions.
L1313: Building on these results, several promising directions for future research emerge. One avenue is to extend the analytical study of aspiration-based dynamics, examining factors that influence convergence rates and the trajectories of aspirations, which simulations suggest usually linger near supersets of the core, often close to socially optimal outcomes. Another direction is to broaden the scope of cooperative game settings.
L1314: The simplicity of the proposed dynamics makes them natural candidates for extension to additional frameworks, such as coalitional games with overlapping coalitions or preference-driven hedonic games. In addition, examining how externalities shape coalition structures, both cardinally and ordinally, presents a compelling opportunity for a deeper investigation.
L1315: Finally, testing these mechanisms in real-world environments could further sharpen the theoretical understanding and validate their practical applicability.
L1316: Our results show that limited information and simple decision-making need not undermine stability in cooperative settings: aspiration-based dynamics, built on simple local rules, can converge to stable outcomes. This demonstrates that complex coordination can arise from modest interactions without global oversight, and that classical concepts like the core remain relevant when reinterpreted through distributed, adaptive dynamics for practical multi-agent systems.

L33:   * cite16†Explore all metrics L34: ## Abstract
L35: We study evolutionary dynamics in assignment games where many agents interact anonymously at virtually no cost. The process is decentralized, very little information is available and trade takes place at many different prices simultaneously. We propose a completely uncoupled learning process that selects a subset of the core of the game with a natural equity interpretation.
L36: This happens even though agents have no knowledge of other agents’ strategies, payoffs, or the structure of the game, and there is no central authority with such knowledge either. In our model, agents randomly encounter other agents, make bids and offers for potential partnerships and match if the partnerships are profitable. Equity is favored by our dynamics because it is more stable, not because of any ex ante fairness criterion.

L15: cite10†View PDF cite11†HTML (experimental) L16: > Abstract:We study fair allocation of profit (or cost) for three central problems from combinatorial optimization: Max-Flow, MST and $b$-matching. The essentially unequivocal choice of solution concept for this purpose would be the core, because of its highly desirable properties. However, recent work [Vaz24] observed that for the assignment game, an arbitrary core imputation makes no fairness guarantee at the level of individual agents.
L17: To rectify this deficiency, special core imputations, called equitable core imputations, were defined - there are two such imputations, leximin and leximax - and efficient algorithms were given for finding them. For all three games, we start by giving examples to show that an arbitrary core imputation can be excessively unfair to certain agents. This led us to seek equitable core imputations for our three games as well.
L18: However, the ubiquitous tractable vs intractable schism separates the assignment game from our three games, making our task different from that of [Vaz24]. As is usual in the presence of intractability, we resorted to defining the Owen set for each game and algorithmically relating it to the set of optimal dual solutions of the underlying combinatorial problem. We then give polynomial time algorithms for finding equitable imputations in the Owen set.
L19: The motivation for this work is two-fold: the emergence of automated decision-making, with a special emphasis on fairness, and the plethora of industrial applications of our three games.

L11@P1: Abstract
L12@P1: For each assignment market, an associated bargaining problem is defined and some
L13@P1: bargaining solutions to this problem are analyzed. For a particular choice of the disagreement point, the Nash solution and the Kalai–Smorodinsky solution coincide and give the
L14@P1: midpoint between the buyers-optimal core allocation and the sellers-optimal core allocation, and thus they belong to the core. Moreover, under the assumption that all agents
L15@P1: in the market are active, the subset of core allocations that can be obtained as a KalaiSmorodinsky solution, from some suitable disagreement point, is characterized as the set
L16@P1: of stable allocations where each agent is paid at least half of his maximum core payoff.
L17@P1: All allocations in this last set can also be obtained by a negotiation procedure `a la Nash.

L25@P2: The aim of this paper is to make a connection between cooperative games in coalitional form
L26@P2: and cooperative bargaining theory, for a particular situation which is that of the bilateral
L27@P2: assignment markets.
L28@P2: In a bilateral assignment market a product that comes in indivisible units is exchanged
L29@P2: for money, and each participant either supplies or demands exactly one unit. The units need
L30@P2: not be alike and the same unit may have different values for different participants. From
L31@P2: these valuations, a matrix can be defined which reflects the profit that can be obtained by
L32@P2: each buyer-seller pair if they trade.
L33@P2: Assuming that side payments are allowed, Shapley and Shubik (1972) define the assignment game as a cooperative model for this bilateral market. In this model, utility is identified
L34@P2: with money, and so an allocation is a vector of incomes such that the sum of payoffs of each
L35@P2: optimally matched pair equals the output of that pairing. Moreover, an allocation is stable if
L36@P2: no agent can match a different partner in such a way that the output of this pairing exceeds
L37@P2: the sum of their payoffs. They prove that the core of the assignment game coincides with the
L38@P2: set of stable allocations and is always nonempty.
L39@P2: The necessity of an analysis of the bargaining possibilities inherent in an assignment
L40@P2: market is already highlighted in the work of Shapley and Shubik. As far as we know, the first

L6@P0: Abstract
L7@P0: We study fair allocation of profit (or cost) for three central problems from combinatorial
L8@P0: optimization: Max-Flow, MST and b-matching. The essentially unequivocal choice of solution
L9@P0: concept for this purpose would be the core, because of its highly desirable properties . However,
L10@P0: recent work [Vaz24] observed that for the assignment game, an arbitrary core imputation makes
L11@P0: no fairness guarantee at the level of individual agents. To rectify this deficiency, special core
L12@P0: imputations, called equitable core imputations, were defined — there are two such imputations,
L13@P0: leximin and leximax — and efficient algorithms were given for finding them.
L14@P0: For all three games, we start by giving examples to show that an arbitrary core imputation
L15@P0: can be excessively unfair to certain agents. This led us to seek equitable core imputations for
L16@P0: our three games as well. However, the ubiquitous tractable vs intractable schism separates the
L17@P0: assignment game from our three games, making our task different from that of [Vaz24]. As is
L18@P0: usual in the presence of intractability, we resorted to defining the Owen set for each game and
L19@P0: algorithmically relating it to the set of optimal dual solutions of the underlying combinatorial
L20@P0: problem. We then give polynomial time algorithms for finding equitable imputations in the
L21@P0: Owen set.
L22@P0: The motivation for this work is two-fold: the emergence of automated decision-making, with
L23@P0: a special emphasis on fairness, and the plethora of industrial applications of our three games.

L28@P1: With automated decision-making emerging as the norm, the design of algorithms which ensure fair
L29@P1: allocations to agents has become increasingly important; these are not only ethical, but also lead
L30@P1: to customer satisfaction, and hence loyalty, to businesses paying attention to this issue. In this
L31@P1: vein, our paper studies the fair allocation of profit or cost for three problems : Max-Flow, MST
L32@P1: and b-matching. All three are central to combinatorial optimization, with a plethora of industrial
L33@P1: applications , e.g., see [Wai94], [AMO93] and [Sch86]. The corresponding games, which distribute
L34@P1: profit (or cost), have also received considerable attention in economics and computer science, e.g.,
L35@P1: see [Mou14].
L36@P1: As an example, assume that several agents have built pipes for carrying flow from a source to a
L37@P1: sink and the resulting profit needs to be distributed among the agents. What is a disciplined way
L38@P1: of doing this? The gold standard solution concept in this regard is that of the core which gives each
L39@P1: sub-coalition at least as much profit as its inherent worth, hence ensuring that no sub-coalition has
L40@P1: incentive to secede, see details in Section 1.1. However as pointed out recently, for the assignment
L41@P1: game [Vaz24], an arbitrary core imputation makes no fairness guarantee at the level of individual
L42@P1: agents. Similarly, for the three games stated above, we give examples in Section 3.1.4 to show that
L43@P1: an arbitrary core imputation can be excessively unfair to certain agents. This led us to studying
L44@P1: equitable core imputations, proposed in [Vaz24], which comprise of two special imputations in the
L45@P1: core: leximin and leximax.
L46@P1: The first work to seek a middle ground in the tension between sub-coalitions demanding profit
L47@P1: which is commensurate with their inherent worth and the societal norm of “equality”, was the
L48@P1: well-known egalitarian solution of Dutta and Ray [DR89]. For a convex game1, this is the unique
L49@P1: core imputation which Lorenz dominates all other core imputations. At a high level, our goal, and
L50@P1: that of [Vaz24], is analogous to that of Dutta and Ray. Section 1.1 states three shortcomings of
L51@P1: the approach of [DR89] as well as the way they are rectified via the approach of [Vaz24] and the
L52@P1: current paper.
L53@P1: The ubiquitous tractable vs intractable schism separates the assignment game from our three
L54@P1: games, making our task different from that of [Vaz24]. The core of the assignment game consists
L55@P1: of all optimal solutions to the dual of the LP-relaxation of the maximum weight matching problem

L60@P1: establish a weaker evidence of intractability2, see Section 7.

L72@P2: Results and key ideas:
L73@P2: 1. For the max-flow game, we show that every optimal solution to the dual LP efficiently leads
L74@P2: to an imputation in the Owen set. Furthermore, we give a polynomial time algorithm for
L75@P2: determining if a given imputation belongs to the Owen set and if so, finding a corresponding
L76@P2: optimal dual solution - the analogous result for the b-matching game was given in [SLJ01].
L77@P2: 2. For the MST game, we show that every optimal solution to the dual LP efficiently yields a
L78@P2: set of core imputations, hence characterizing its Owen set. Among the various primal-dual
L79@P2: formulations for the MST game, we establish that the minimum branching LP serves as the
L80@P2: right formulation for defining the Owen set. Despite its exponentially many dual variables on
L81@P2: sets, we provide an elegant interpretation that maps them to costs on agents. We also provide
L82@P2: a separation oracle that facilitates the use of the ellipsoid method for efficiently verifying core
L83@P2: membership. Because the procedure uses ellipsoid algorithm, it is not practical; we leave the
L84@P2: open problem of finding efficient combinatorial algorithms.
L85@P2: 3. We give a combinatorial, strongly polynomial algorithm for finding the leximin and leximax
L86@P2: core imputations in the Owen set of the max-flow game. Our approach leverages the PicardQueyranne structure to efficiently compute dual optimal solutions corresponding to these
L87@P2: imputations. For the b-matching game, we do the same by building on the algorithms of
L88@P2: [Vaz24].
L89@P2: 4. For the MST (and more generally, minimum branching) game, we give LP-based polynomial
L90@P2: time algorithms, using the ellipsoid method, for finding the leximin and leximax imputations
L91@P2: in the Owen set. Again we leave the open problem of finding combinatorial polynomial time
L92@P2: algorithms.
L93@P2: 1.1 Background information
L94@P2: The core distributes the total worth of a game among the agents in such a way that the profit
L95@P2: received by a sub-coalition is at least as large as the profit which the sub-coalition can generate
L96@P2: all by itself. This not only ensures stability of the grand coalition, since no sub-coalition has an
L97@P2: incentive to secede, but ensure some degree of fairness, namely to each of exponentially many subcoalitions – a stringent requirement indeed. Additionally, the core also provides profound insights
L98@P2: into the negotiating power of individuals and sub-coalitions, see [Mou14, Vaz22] and Remark 5.6.
L99@P2: However, as pointed out recently in the context of the assignment game [Vaz24], which forms a
L100@P2: paradigmatic setting for studying the core — in large part due to the classic work of Shapley and
L101@P2: Shubik [SS71] — an arbitrary core imputation makes no fairness guarantee at the level of individual
L102@P2: agents. This is due to the fact that a singleton sub-coalition (or a set of players from the same side
L103@P2: of the bipartition), can make zero profit, and therefore its profit under a core imputation can be
L104@P2: an arbitrary amount.
L105@P2: It is well know that “fairness” can be defined in many ways, depending on the setting. Among
L106@P2: these, the use of max-min and min-max fairness is widespread, e.g., in game theory, networking
L107@P2: and resource allocation. A leximin allocation maximizes the smallest component and subject to
L108@P2: that, it maximizes the second smallest, and so on. It therefore goes much further than a max-min
L109@P2-3: 3allocation. Similarly a leximax allocation goes much further than a min-max allocation. [Vaz24]
L110@P3: defined leximin and leximax core imputations as equitable core imputations. These two imputations
L111@P3: achieve equality in different ways: whereas leximin tries to make poor agents more rich, leximax
L112@P3: tries to make rich agents less rich, thereby indirectly making poor agents more rich, hence they
L113@P3: may be better suited for different applications.
L114@P3: The egalitarian solution of Dutta and Ray [DR89] has three shortcomings: it does not apply to
L115@P3: several key natural games, including the assignment, MST and max-flow games, since they are not
L116@P3: convex; it is not efficiently computable for any non-trivial, natural game; and the Lorenz order is a
L117@P3: partial, and not a total, order. As stated above, [Vaz24] and our work rectify all three shortcomings.

L122@P3: where not all dual variables represent shadow prices, and the prices have to be carefully defined
L123@P3: from the dual optimal solutions. Thus, this definition provides a more inclusive framework.
L124@P3: [SZ84] explored Owen set imputations, referring to them as the set of dual payoffs. While Owen
L125@P3: set generally represents a subset of core imputations, [SZ84] outlined conditions under which the

L124@P3: [SZ84] explored Owen set imputations, referring to them as the set of dual payoffs. While Owen
L125@P3: set generally represents a subset of core imputations, [SZ84] outlined conditions under which the
L126@P3: core and Owen set coincide. For instance, in max-flow games with unit capacity edges, one of
L127@P3: the conditions from [SZ84] is met, allowing our algorithms to return the leximin fair imputation
L128@P3: among all core sets. However, this is not universally true. As we will show in later sections, finding
L129@P3: a leximin imputation among the core set is NP-hard in a general max-flow game. However we
L130@P3: will provide efficient algorithms for finding a leximin fair imputation among the Owen set. In
L131@P3: some special classes of flow and assignment games, [GG92] showed the leximin core can be found
L132@P3: efficiently. Our work is closely related, as we extend the analysis to the general class of max-flow
L133@P3: games.
L134@P3: Extensive research has been conducted on finding fair cost-shares in a minimum spanning tree
L135@P3: (MST) game that is a special subcase of the min-cost branching game. [GH81] showed that the
L136@P3: core of an MST game is never empty. Efficient procedures for computing core imputations and
L137@P3: the nucleolus were later developed, see [GH84]. [Bir76] introduced a cost-sharing rule that ensures
L138@P3: each agent’s cost share is within the core by distributing costs proportional to their connection
L139@P3: costs to the MST. However, this rule may not yield a unique cost share in cases with multiple
L140@P3: MSTs. [ABBG06] proposed two methods to find fair core imputations within the subset governed
L141@P3: by Bird’s rule. Our work, in contrast, adopts a broader definition of fairness in the class of Owen
L142@P3: set imputations, which extends beyond Bird’s rule.
L143@P3: Besides Bird’s rule, several other solutions have been proposed to allocate costs among individuals in a minimum cost network, including methods by [Kar02], Folk [FTM94] [BVP07], Cyclecomplete[Tru12], a family of strict responsive rules [BM10], or the class of egalitarian Shapley value
L144@P3: solutions [CH13]. Most of these solutions consider all relevant link costs for determining the final
L145@P3: imputation of optimal costs. Contrary to conventional approaches, [GGPS20] introduced a model
L146@P3: where only a subset of network costs is considered, assuming agents possess localized knowledge
L147@P3: with limited relevant information. They proposed a novel egalitarian approach to cost-share in
L148@P3-4: minimum cost spanning games, reinterpreting spanning tree cost-share as a claims problem. How4ever, due to its focus on local perspectives, their method does not always satisfy core properties.
L149@P4: In their subsequent work [GGPS22], the same authors developed new methods for distributing
L150@P4: optimal network costs by framing each minimum cost spanning tree scenario as a claims problem
L151@P4: and applying corresponding rules. However, similar to their earlier research, these methods do
L152@P4: not guarantee core imputations. In contrast, we present an efficient algorithm that computes a
L153@P4: leximin/leximax fair Owen set imputation, without imposing restrictions on agent assumptions. A
L154@P4: couple of studies have explored some variations of the problem; [ZCZ20] studied cost sharing in
L155@P4: MST games without a source node and proved that the core is non-empty. [LNB16] introduced
L156@P4: the Generalized Minimum Spanning Tree Game, showing that the core might be empty. [BVP21]
L157@P4: provides an exhaustive review of papers addressing the cost sharing problem in MST games.
L158@P4: In b-matching games, [Sot92] showed that the core is non-empty. [SSLGJ01] and [Vaz23] demonstrated that any optimal dual LP solution is a core imputation, though these imputations do not
L159@P4: fully characterize the core for b-matching games as they do for assignment games. [Vaz24] recently
L160@P4: proposed a combinatorial algorithm for finding the leximin/leximax core of the assignment game,
L161@P4: and we show that with modifications, it can be utilized to find the leximin/leximax Owen set imputation in b-matching games. [BKPW18] proved that core membership testing in edge-constrained
L162@P4: b-matching is co-NP-complete, and very recently, [GTV25] proved this for standard b-matching
L163@P4: game as well.
L164@P4: In cooperative game theory, the nucleolus is a solution concept related to the core and fair
L165@P4: imputations, designed to balance dissatisfaction among coalitions by minimizing the maximum
L166@P4: dissatisfaction lexicographically. Unlike the core, which can sometimes be empty, the nucleolus
L167@P4: always exists. [Sch69] showed that when the core is non-empty, the nucleolus belongs to the
L168@P4: core. [SR94] provided an efficient algorithm for determining the nucleolus in assignment games.
L169@P4: However, for general cooperative games including the three games studied in this paper, there
L170@P4: is no known polynomial-time algorithm for finding the nucleolus - it is in fact NP-hard for both
L171@P4: MST games([FKK98]) and max-flow games([DFS06]). This challenge motivates the exploration of
L172@P4: alternative fairness concepts, such as the leximin/leximax core employed in this paper. In general,
L173@P4: the leximin/leximax core imputation does not coincide with the nucleolus. Nevertheless, [GG92]
L174@P4: demonstrated that under specific conditions in max-flow games, the leximin core and the nucleolus
L175@P4: are equivalent.

L274@P6: 3.1.4 Unfair imputations for these games
L275@P6: In each of these games, there are core imputations that may be considered very unfair. For example,
L276@P6: in the max-flow game, consider a path of n unit-capacity edges from the source to the sink. An
L277@P6: imputation that allocates all the profit to a single edge while giving nothing to the others is in
L278@P6: the core, but a fairer imputation would distribute the profit equally among all edges, giving each a
L279@P6: share of 1/n.
L280@P6: Similarly, in the MST game, imagine n vertices connected to the root by a path of n unitcost edges. An imputation that charges all the cost to the farthest vertex is in the core, but
L281@P6: a more equitable choice would be to charge each agent one unit of cost. Shapley and Shubik
L282@P6: ([SS71]]) demonstrated that in the assignment game, a special case of b-matching game, the set of
L283@P6-7: 7core imputations corresponds precisely to the optimal solutions of the dual LP-relaxation of the
L284@P7: maximum weight matching problem. Moreover, they showed that this set of core imputations forms
L285@P7: a lattice, where the extreme points tend to disproportionately favor one side.

L308: In this section we intend to compute the set of extreme core allocations or, equivalently, extreme competitive salary vectors of the many-to-one assignment markets. L41: Cooperative games model strategic settings in which agents coordinate to form partnerships and share payoffs to achieve mutually beneficial outcomes. These settings range from pairwise matchings to larger groups forming coalitions. In this paper, we address two setups of cooperative games: transferable utility coalitional games and bipartite B-matchings.
L42: For both settings, we propose distributed dynamics where agents form and break partnerships according to evolving internal aspiration levels that reflect self-interest. Our distributed dynamics require simple computations, limited memory, and minimal knowledge of the environment. We prove that these dynamics converge to stable outcomes analogous to the core, where no group of agents has an incentive to deviate from the proposed partnerships.
L43: We illustrate our dynamics through computational experiments on exchange networks. The simulations exhibit resilient behavior of the algorithms under message drops between the agents and dynamic entry and exit of agents.

L65: Cooperative game theory is a branch of game theory that models strategic interactions in multi-agent settings where agents can benefit from forming partnerships.
